title: Jitter: Measuring the Loop You Are About to Trust

questions.question: A control loop averages exactly its thousand microsecond period. What has that told you?
options: Almost nothing about whether it ever misses a deadline
That it never misses a deadline
That its worst case is close to a thousand microseconds
That the scheduler is treating it fairly
questions.explanation: A loop can be early or on time ninety nine times and four milliseconds late on the hundredth, and still average perfectly. The average is the one summary that cannot see a tail.

questions.question: What is the difference between the interval and the lateness of a cycle?
options: The interval is the time since the previous run, the lateness is that minus the period it was meant to be
They are two names for the same measurement
The interval is measured from the start of the loop, the lateness from the previous cycle
Lateness is the interval expressed as a percentage
questions.explanation: Lateness is the quantity a controller cares about, because it is the amount by which the time it integrated over differs from the time it assumed.

questions.question: Why a fixed array of counters rather than keeping every sample?
options: Keeping every sample allocates without bound inside the loop being measured, which changes what is measured
An array of counters is more accurate
Samples cannot be stored in a vector
It uses less memory, and nothing else follows from it
questions.explanation: The instrument has to be cheaper than the thing it measures. Recording into a histogram is an index calculation and an increment, with no allocation however long it runs.

questions.question: A sample lands beyond the last bucket. Clamping the index to the last bucket keeps the access in bounds. What does it cost?
options: The worst case now reads as the top of the range no matter how far past it the sample was
Nothing, it is the standard approach
One sample is lost from the count
The median becomes wrong
questions.explanation: The histogram understates the outlier in proportion to how bad it was, so it fails hardest where the answer matters most. Count overflows separately and keep the true worst value. See E-RT-0001.

questions.question: A loop specification says the 99.9th percentile is under 200 microseconds and nothing exceeds 500. Why is that better than an average?
options: It constrains the tail, which is the part that misses deadlines
It is a stricter number
Percentiles are easier to measure than averages
It avoids floating point
questions.explanation: A specification written as an average is not a specification, because the tail is unconstrained and the tail is the entire question.

questions.question: Your loop's tail is hundreds of microseconds. Which cause should you rule out first?
options: Your own code, an allocation or a lock or a log line inside the loop
The kernel scheduler
Processor frequency scaling
Page faults on first touch
questions.explanation: All four cause tails, and the kernel is the interesting answer, which is exactly why it is the wrong one to reach for first. The cheapest thing to check is what the loop itself does.
